--- order: 2 unit: layers node: AC9TDI10K02 n3 assumes: [web-layers] title: Why keep them apart summary: "Keeping content, structure and presentation apart lets each change on its own: one style sheet restyles a whole site, the same page fits a phone or a laptop, and a screen reader can tell a blind reader what each part is. A page that fakes its structure with looks works for nobody but sighted readers." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Two pages look almost the same. To a blind student using a screen reader, one of them has no headings at all. How?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8487 url: http://127.0.0.1:8487/index.html readySelector: ".wdview" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: web.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Page B: the same words as the club page, styled with big bold text instead of headings and a list." } explainClip: query: { code: "@web.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "What a screen reader hears" say: "Two pages that look almost the same." clip: - click: "Screen reader, off" - caption: { text: "Page A: \"Heading level 1\", \"Navigation\", \"List, 3 items\". The structure is read out.", say: "On page A, the screen reader announces headings, the menu and a list." } - wait: 1600 - click: Page B - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "Page B" } - caption: { text: "Page B looks similar, but it is just lines of text: no headings, no list, nothing to jump to.", say: "Page B is just lines of text. The look was faked." } - wait: 1800 --- In *Three layers* each layer could change on its own. That isn't just tidy: it decides who can use a page, on what device, and how much work it takes to change a whole site. ## Predict: what the screen reader says ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to what a screen reader announces tests the new move: tools read the structure, not the look." check: type: predict q: "Page A marks \"This week\" with a heading tag. Page B makes it big and bold with no heading tag. Both look almost the same. What does a screen reader say for Page B?" options: ["Just the words \"This week\", like any other text", "\"Heading level 2: This week\", the same as Page A", "\"Big bold text: This week\"", "Nothing at all"] actual: "Just the words. A screen reader reads the structure; on Page B there is no heading to announce, so a blind reader can't jump between sections." ``` ## Try: listen to both pages ```step stage: run insight: "Hearing both pages through the screen reader settles the prediction: same look, different structure, different experience." try: { playground: board, starter: "web.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Turn on the screen reader and listen to Page A, then Page B. What is missing from Page B?", when: "j >= 2", explain: "Headings, the navigation and the list. Page B only looks structured." } ``` Was your prediction right? ## Worked example: three reasons ```step stage: investigate insight: "Working through three situations models the new move: each benefit comes from one layer changing while the others stay. Sam judges a page by its look, the misconception planted after the method." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A school site has 200 pages, all using one style sheet. How many files must change to make every heading green?" answer: "1" feedback: - ["200", "The pages all link to the same style sheet."] explain: "One rule in one file: h2 { color: green; } restyles all 200 pages." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#sam" text: "Sam compares Page A and Page B. Click the line where it first goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: same-look-same-page explain: "Line 4: a screen reader, a search engine and a phone layout use the structure, not the look. Page B's visitors who can't see it get no headings and no list." - check: type: question q: "Why can the same page appear in one column on a phone and two on a laptop?" options: ["The presentation changes with the screen size; the content and structure stay the same", "The website keeps a separate copy for phones", "The phone rewrites the HTML", "It can't; phones show the laptop layout"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "One page, different style rules for different widths.", "The structure isn't touched.", "Most sites do change layout."] explain: "CSS can say \"on narrow screens, one column\": a presentation choice." ``` ### Separation pays off ```worked \text{a whole site} :: One style sheet styles every page: change a rule once, every page changes. \text{a phone} :: The same content and structure; different presentation rules for a narrow screen. \text{a screen reader} :: It reads the structure aloud (headings, lists, menus) and ignores the look. \text{editing} :: Writers change content, designers change presentation, without breaking each other's work. ``` Now count the files for the 200-page site. ### Find the mistake ### Phone or laptop ## Vary: one change, many effects ```step stage: modify insight: "Each task changes one thing and watches what follows: one CSS rule across a site, the screen width, then the style sheet off with the screen reader on." try: { playground: board, starter: "web.yml#site", height: 680 } tasks: - starter: "web.yml#site" check: { type: board, text: "Change one rule in the style sheet so the headings change colour. Watch the other pages of the site.", when: "c >= 1 and w = 1 and u = 1", explain: "Every page that uses the style sheet changed at once, and no HTML was touched." } - starter: "web.yml#phone" check: { type: board, text: "Switch to phone width. Did the content or structure change?", when: "v = 1", explain: "No: the same words and tags, laid out narrower. The presentation adapts." } - starter: "web.yml#phone" check: { type: board, text: "Switch the style sheet off and the screen reader on. Does the screen reader change?", when: "p = 0 and r = 1", explain: "Not at all: it never used the look. Structure is what carries meaning." } ``` ### A whole site ### Phone ### No style at all ## Practise: why it matters ```step stage: practise insight: "Explaining separation in new situations is the same move in mixed forms, plus a review of the three layers." tasks: - check: type: question q: "A designer puts and tags all through a 50-page site to make it look right. A year later the school changes its colours. What happens?" options: ["Someone edits all 50 pages by hand", "One style sheet change fixes it", "The colours update themselves", "Nothing needs changing"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "There is no shared style sheet to change.", "The look is written into each page.", "The old colours are written into every page."] explain: "With the look mixed into the HTML, every page must be edited. Kept in CSS, it's one change." - check: type: question q: "Which helps a blind student most?" options: ["Real headings and lists in the HTML", "Large, colourful text", "More pictures", "A bigger screen"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The screen reader ignores size and colour.", "Pictures need text descriptions too.", "They aren't looking at the screen."] explain: "The screen reader announces the structure, so headings and lists let them jump around the page." - check: type: question q: "Review:
around the menu links is which layer?" options: ["Structure", "Content", "Presentation"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The link words are content; the tag says what the part is.", "It doesn't change the look by itself."] explain: "It marks the part as navigation: structure." ``` ### A site-wide change ### Screen readers ### Review: layers ## Make: fix Page B ```step stage: make insight: "Repairing a page whose structure was faked with looks reverses the process: from what each part should be to the tags that say so." try: { playground: board, starter: "web.yml#make", height: 700 } hint: ["Turn on the screen reader: what should be headings and a list?", "Swap the bold title lines for `

` and `

`, and the three event lines for a `
    ` with `
  • ` items.", "Take out every ``, `` and `
    `; the style sheet does the look."] check: { type: board, text: "Fix Page B's HTML: real headings and a real list, no tags used only for looks, and the same words.", when: "x = 1 and d = 1", explain: "Now the screen reader announces the headings and the list, and the style sheet can make it look like anything. Structure first, looks second." } ``` Then: on a real website, use your browser's reader view. What does it keep, and what does it throw away? ```teacher summary: Students hear two look-alike pages through a screen reader, restyle a three-page site with one CSS rule, view a page at phone width, and fix a page whose structure was faked with looks (AC9TDI10K02 node 3), with no coding needed beyond tidying tags. time: 45 timing: Predict and Try 7 min · Worked example 10 min · Vary 10 min · Practise 6 min · Make 12 min goals: - I can explain why content, structure and presentation are kept apart. - "I can give examples: a whole site, a phone, a screen reader." - I can fix a page whose headings and lists were faked with looks. struggle: "The Make asks students to edit HTML for the first time in this course. It is hard on purpose but small: the screen reader shows what's missing; let them use it rather than giving the tags." before: > Try the boards yourself. The one idea: separation lets each layer change on its own, which is what makes sites maintainable, adaptable and accessible. The accessibility point matters most to many students; a short screen reader demo (VoiceOver on a Mac or iPad, Narrator on Windows) on a real page lands it. The board's screen reader is a simplified model: it announces headings, links, lists and landmarks, as real screen readers do, but real ones say much more. Page B (the "messy" page) uses tags that are still found on old sites (font, b, br for layout); they work but carry no meaning. running: - 'Predict: students who chose "Heading level 2" for Page B think the reader sees the look.' - 'Try: ask a student to describe how they would find "Coming up" on Page B without seeing it.' - "Worked example: ask who else reads structure: search engines, translation tools, reader view." - "Vary: after one rule restyles three pages, ask how that would go with 200 pages styled by hand." - "Make: listen to the fixed page together in the screen reader." stuck: - see: A student says the two pages are the same (Sam's mistake). ask: Turn on the screen reader for both. What does each say first? fix: "Same look, different structure: not the same page for everyone." - see: A student's fixed page still shows tags used only for looks. ask: Which tags are left? Which part should each be? fix: Replace b and font with h1 or h2; turn the br lines into li items in a ul. stretch: Look up the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). Find one rule that is about structure and one about presentation. support: "A list of the structure tags they need for the Make: h1, h2, p, ul, li, nav." leads: > Links: Code › HTML & CSS (sections, components and the club page put this to work); Security and privacy (what a page gives away, planned). exit: q: Give two reasons to keep a page's look in a style sheet instead of in its HTML. a: "For example: one change restyles a whole site; screen readers and phones use the structure, so the page works for more people and devices." explain: > Keeping the layers apart means each one can change on its own: - **A whole site**: one style sheet styles every page, so one change restyles them all. - **Phones**: the same content and structure get different presentation on a small screen. - **Screen readers**: they read the structure aloud (headings, lists, menus), so a heading faked with big bold text is just plain text to a blind reader. Structure says what each part is; presentation only says how it looks. class: inquiry: q: Two pages look the same. Why might one still be worse? prompts: - Who else reads a page? - What do they read? notes: Screen readers and search use structure. Style alone can't carry meaning. activities: - at: predict kind: activity title: Hear the page minutes: 5 do: > One student reads Page B as a screen reader would: just the words, no headings. The rest try to find 'This week' by ear alone. notes: With no headings there is nothing to jump between. - at: make kind: discussion title: Change the look minutes: 3 do: > Say how you'd change every page on a site to a new colour with one edit. What has to be true? notes: The style sits in one place, apart from the structure. questions: - at: investigate title: Why structure? type: question q: Why mark a heading as a heading instead of only making it big? options: - Programs and readers can find it - It loads faster - It looks bolder - It uses less memory answer: 0 explain: Structure is what programs read; looks are for eyes. ```

# region: sam

Page B uses big bold text for "This week".
On screen they look almost the same.
